catalog_quote: No two consonants ever stand together, and there are therefore no closed syllables. ... There is no fixed rule for Accent or Stress. Usually it is on the penultimate (i.e., the last syllable but one), but the exceptions are numerous, and can be learned only by listening to the conversation of Motu people. Motu is a less strongly accented language than English, and beginners should endeavour to pronounce it as smoothly and evenly as possible. The accent may affect the number of a very few nouns, e.g., hahine, woman: hahine, women, kekeni, girl; kekeni, girls ... As noted in Section 1, a very few nouns indicate number by accent; e.g., hahine, woman; hahine, women; kekeni, girl; kekeni, girls. ... Note. -- It is probable that those nouns in which plural is now indicated by accent originally came under this duplication rule.

new_statements.quote: As a rule the accent is on the penultima; but there are exceptions. When suffixes are added the accent is shifted forward, as hahìne, hahinèna, mèro meròna. Reduplicated words have the two accents of the simple form, as kadàra kadàra-kadàra. The natives of Tupuseleia, Kapakapa, and Gaile are known by the peculiarity of raising the voice on the last syllable of the sentence.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog row for Motu (catalog-all-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; Lawes supplies the placement: penultimate accent by rule, with suffix-shift and reduplication detail.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the penultimate syllable as the general rule, with unspecified exceptions; accent is recomputed on the suffixed word (hahìne > hahinèna, mèro > meròna), so it stays penultimate in the whole word; each half of a reduplicated word keeps its own accent (kadàra-kadàra).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; reduplicated words 'have the two accents of the simple form' (kadàra kadàra-kadàra), i.e. both halves accented.
new_statements.exceptions: 'but there are exceptions' (none listed). Sentence-final rising voice noted as a dialect trait of Tupuseleia, Kapakapa and Gaile (intonation, not word stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Lawes 1896 describes the Motu of Port Moresby, Pari, Borebada, Lealea, Manumanu and neighbouring villages and notes 'considerable local differences in pronunciation' (p. 1); his sentence-final voice-raising remark concerns the Tupuseleia, Kapakapa and Gaile speakers and is intonation, not word stress. Taylor 1970 is explicitly the Tupuseleia dialect (informants Mahuta Kariko, Renagi Lohia, Rage Tau, all from Tupuseleia, pp. 21-22; section 6.6 'Tupuseleian Motu').

new_statements.quote: Only major rules are given. To these there are exceptions, some of which may be able to be handled by minor rules, others may have to be marked individually. Another problem is that on words formed by total reduplication (in particular) the position of the primary stress, which is not heavy, may vary. [...] There is one primary stress in each word. [...] (a) If there are two diphthongs then the stress falls on the vowel in the first. [ˈgaygay] 'snake' (b) If only one diphthong occurs then the vowel in it is stressed. [kuˈdow] 'heart' [ˈvaoha] 'sea-urchin' (c) If there is no diphthong the stress falls on the second last vowel. [ˈia] 'he' [ˈhua] 'moon' [ˈara] 'fence' [ˈlahi] 'fire' [huˈala] 'crocodile' [hiˈsiu] 'star' (d) If there is only one vowel it takes the stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty. Taylor's rule (c) agrees with Lawes's penultimate default and with Lawes's suffix shift; it adds the diphthong-attraction clauses (a)-(b), a secondary-stress rule, initial-stress exceptions, and the verb-root/transitivizer stress pattern. Describes the Tupuseleia dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word, not heavy. A diphthong (vowel + glide) attracts primary stress: with two diphthongs the first is stressed, with one that one is stressed; otherwise stress falls on the second-last vowel (penult); monosyllables are stressed. Suffixes: two-vowel words move stress to the last root vowel ([ˈdika] 'bad' > [diˈka+na], [ˈlata] > [laˈta+dia]); words of four or more vowels keep stress on the second-last vowel; a stressed vowel followed by a glide keeps stress under suffixation ([ˈvayra+na] 'his face'). Verbs: primary stress on a vowel of the verb root, except that the transitivizing suffixes -heni, -tani, -lai and directional/manner/degree adverbs (iti 'up', namonamo, mate) take it (p. 237).
new_statements.secondary_stress: PR19 Secondary Stress Rule (p. 235): 'If two vowels precede the vowel with the primary stress then the first vowel receives the secondary stress. If only one vowel precedes it, then that vowel receives the secondary stress.' E.g. [ˌaˈgeva] 'string of beads', [ˌduˈbara] 'a crab', [ˌkuˈdou] 'heart', [ˌkakaˈkaka] 'red'. In initial-stressed reduplications the first vowel of the second half takes secondary stress ([ˈmeroˌmero] 'little boy', [ˈhuaˌhua] 'fruit').
new_statements.exceptions: Words of four or more vowels (mostly total reduplications) may take primary stress on the first vowel instead, and some allow both patterns ([ˌkakaˈkaka] or [ˈkakaˌkaka] 'red'); a number of three-vowel words without diphthongs have initial primary stress ([ˈherea] 'very', [ˈhereva] 'to speak'); other exceptions 'may have to be marked individually'.
new_statements.identity_note: Lawes 1896 describes the Motu of Port Moresby, Pari, Borebada, Lealea, Manumanu and neighbouring villages and notes 'considerable local differences in pronunciation' (p. 1); his sentence-final voice-raising remark concerns the Tupuseleia, Kapakapa and Gaile speakers and is intonation, not word stress. Taylor 1970 is explicitly the Tupuseleia dialect (informants Mahuta Kariko, Renagi Lohia, Rage Tau, all from Tupuseleia, pp. 21-22; section 6.6 'Tupuseleian Motu').

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. Lawes 1896 (the listed work) gives penultimate accent 'as a rule' with unnamed exceptions; Taylor 1970 (already held by the project, read as an extra) makes the same penultimate default explicit as clause (c) but adds that diphthongs (vowel + glide) attract primary stress ([ˈvaoha] 'sea-urchin', [kuˈdow] 'heart'), that some three-vowel words and many total reduplications take initial primary stress, and that stress is 'not heavy'. Both agree stress is recomputed on suffixed words (Lawes hahìne > hahinèna; Taylor [ˈdika] > [diˈka+na]). The two differ only in granularity: a catalog coder following Lawes alone would write fixed: penultimate syllable; following Taylor, weight-sensitive (diphthong-heavy, penult default).

audit.recode_to: Quantity-sensitive penult-default with lexical exceptions: primary stress on the (first) diphthong (V+glide, incl. word-final: kuˈdou 'heart' = final stress) if the word has one, otherwise on the penultimate vowel; what counts as heavy = diphthong/V+glide heavy (no closed syllables, no length); exceptions 'some, lexically marked' (initial stress in some trisyllables e.g. ˈhereva; variable in total reduplications); morphology: suffixes shift stress rightward in two-vowel stems (ˈdika > diˈkana), verb-complex stress on root unless a transitivizer/adverb follows; keep the hahine/kekeni number-by-accent note from Lister-Turner & Clark p. 9/27. Deciding source should become Taylor 1970: 234-237. If the catalog's lexical threshold is 'any residue must be marked individually', lexical-with-weight-sensitive penult-default is the defensible alternative, but what counts as heavy 'not-applicable' and 'no fixed rule' cannot stand against Taylor's PR18.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is in the held archive.org scanned at the stated places (p. 9 lines 391-412; p. 27 lines 1942-1954), verbatim modulo scanned artefacts. (2) The deciding source is an undated learner-oriented 2nd edition of a 1930 missionary grammar; Taylor 1970: 8 (opened) says its sound-system content is essentially Lawes 1896 unchanged. Glottolog lists one true grammar, Taylor 1970 (ANU PhD, xi+298 pp), open at ANU; downloaded and read. Its section 6.5.5 (pp. 234-237, page images read directly because the ClearScan text layer is letter-spaced) replaces 'no fixed rule' with an explicit disjunctive Primary Stress Rule: diphthongs attract stress (first of two; a lone diphthong even word-finally, kuˈdow), else penultimate vowel (huˈala, hiˈsiu), plus a secondary-stress rule, suffix-driven shift in disyllables, verb-complex conditioning, and an acknowledged residue of exceptions
